newsitem.title: FINLAND: MARKETS SEE FEW HELSINKI SUMMIT SURPRISES.
newsitem.headline: MARKETS SEE FEW HELSINKI SUMMIT SURPRISES.

text.p: President Bill Clinton may offer Russia economic sweeteners when he meets President Boris Yeltsin, but analysts said on Wednesday they expect little or no news to emerge which could rattle financial markets.

U.S. officials have signalled increasing support for Russia's demands to be admitted into key economic groups, but analysts say a firm offer of membership of such institutions is unlikely at the Helsinki summit on Thursday and Friday.
Financial markets see events unfurling in Moscow as far more important than any decisions to be taken in the Finnish capital.
"We do not expect anything that is going to impact markets strongly this week," said London-based Merrill Lynch Russia analyst Maxim Shashenkov.
"Russia's future will be solved domestically rather than internationally, so what's going on domestically is several times more important," he told Reuters.
Analysts say Yeltsin's cabinet reshuffle this week, which saw liberal reformers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov handed top jobs, will overshadow any economic news from the summit.
"I do not expect any news that will significantly affect the markets," said Russia analyst Catherine MacDougall at London investment bank Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"The market is becoming less and less sensitive...to politics and macro-economic issues. That's a sign that the Russian market is maturing," she said.
On top of the summit agenda is the issue of NATO enlargement, which Russia bitterly opposes but which the U.S. and its allies are pushing.
"Markets are not very sensitive to Russia-NATO talks and I think the major news of the cabinet reshuffle has been discounted already," MacDougall said.

The U.S. has said it would give Russia an expanded political role in the Group of Seven (G7), the most exclusive club of rich industrialised nations, although Moscow is unlikely to win the full membership it wants.

Clinton may also be prepared to push harder for Russian entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the Paris Club, which discusses debt rescheduling.
At the summit, analysts said Yeltsin will resist any linkage of economic issues and the expansion of NATO.
Instead, the U.S. may work with G7 colleagues to put together a package of measures for the June 20-22 annual G7 summit in Denver.

"What the West is preparing for Russia -- this would be the final package -- is G7, OECD, WTO, closer economic integration," Shashenkov said. "I don't think we'll see any positive surpises in Helsinki. Russia has enough trade-off time until June."
Sergei Arvenyev, of Flemings Securities in London, said even the possibility of the two leaders ending their summit on bad terms would only have a short-term effect on world equities markets.
"For me it's nowhere near in the same league as last week's events with the (Russian) government reshuffle," he said.
